correctness.rationale: For the specified relative one-point game, an abstract move either extends a represented class or creates a new class. At depth t the first kind requires at least t unused points in each represented class independently; the second must use an untouched class of size at least t and leave the depth-(t−1) staircase among the other untouched classes. Conversely, if the depth-t capacities and staircase hold, using a point in the requested represented class or starting a largest untouched class leaves the depth-(t−1) conditions. This proves the exact local equivalence by induction including t=0 and F empty. Summing the row lower bounds forces t(t+1)/2; equality leaves exactly the staircase with distinct sizes, giving the stated multinomial. Enlarging the largest block (for t>0) fills every allowed larger order without increasing the rank beyond t, since only t classes exist. Replayed an independently written profile-game recursion for all partitions of orders 0–12 and all 71,820 choices of occupied sizes in those profiles; it agreed with the formula and the maximum rank at each order.
residual_risks: The replay is corroboration rather than the all-size proof. Only finite structures and the extension game relative to the age of all finite equivalence relations are assessed.

value.rationale: The rank of this non-free-amalgamation age is a natural example and the staircase theorem is informative. But as a standalone increment over the verified broader theorem, the local and global laws are exact substitutions. The extremal size and unique type follow by row summation and equality; the only extra presentation, a multinomial for that same type and the inverse triangular bound, does not leave an independently valuable new finding to repair.
residual_risks: An independently motivated extension beyond the current claim might be valuable; none is asserted here. No historical priority conclusion is needed for this incremental-value assessment.
